Optical networking stocks that powered the AI data-center trade this year are falling fast, and the selling is landing on the group's biggest names at once. Coherent (NYSE:COHR) stock is trading at $209.82, down 12% in afternoon trading, showing how quickly momentum in AI optics has reversed. Selling extends across the AI connectivity supply chain, from laser chips to finished transceiver modules.

TechAnimationStock / Shutterstock.com

Meanwhile, Applied Optoelectronics (NASDAQ:AAOI) stock is at $69.30, down 10%, a slide that lands just behind Coherent's loss. Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE) stock is at $770.53, down 9%. That marks a smaller decline than Coherent and Applied Optoelectronics posted, though still a steep loss for a name that climbed on AI optical demand. Each of these companies sells optical parts that move data inside AI datacenters, so shifts in sentiment toward hyperscaler spending tend to hit Coherent, Applied Optoelectronics and Lumentum shares together.

The Roundhill Photonics & Optics ETF (CBOE:LYTE) is down 10%, falling nearly as hard as Coherent, Applied Optoelectronics and Lumentum. Over in large-cap tech, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 2%, representing a far softer retreat for the NASDAQ 100 benchmark. That gap marks the optics selling as group-wide caution before Coherent, Applied Optoelectronics and Lumentum report quarterly results.

Key Takeaways

Palantir stock rose 7% in the past month as five Wall Street firms, including Goldman Sachs and Barclays, set targets of $230 to $265, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 2%.

A 7% software-wide drop on Oct. 16 had no Palantir news behind it, and the stock won it all back within three sessions as software rallied, with ServiceNow and Datadog up about 11% this month too.

The Street's average target of $206 is now only about 2% above the stock, and its forward P/E sits around its five-year average of 103x.

Third-quarter results on Nov. 2 need to show U.S. commercial growth well above the 134% guide, so holding makes more sense than adding before then.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) is up 7% in the past month, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 2.2%.

Wall Street did much of the lifting, and a 7% software rout mid-month didn't stick. But the stock now sits almost right on the Street's average price target.

Most of the gain came in early October. Within about two days, Daniel Ives's Yorkville Ives & Co started coverage at Buy with a $250 target, Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to Buy at $230, and Barclays started at Buy with a $265 target, the Street's highest.

On Oct. 9, Palantir jumped 5.2% to a record close of $209.05, its first since November 2025.

On Oct. 12, Baird raised its target to $250 from $200. It pointed to how far Palantir can cut the cost of running AI (95% in one defense contractor's use case). Mizuho went to $245 from $215 on Oct. 15. Only Phillip Securities went the other way, cutting the stock to Hold.

A 7% drop that had nothing to do with Palantir

Then came Oct. 16. Palantir fell 7.2% as investors dumped software over worries about AI valuations. The software ETF IGV fell nearly 5%.

There was no Palantir news, but the drop still left the stock 11% below its record, in a correction.

And nothing in the business had changed. Q2 brought a record 220 deals worth $1 million or more, 73 of them over $10 million, and 149% growth in U.S. commercial revenue.

Key Takeaways

Zscaler stock rose 14% in the past month, despite a 10% one-day drop when its chief revenue officer stepped down.

An Investor Day that reaffirmed guidance and set a base case of more than $8 billion of ARR by fiscal 2031 brought a wave of price-target raises.

Critical web-server flaws lifted Zscaler, CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks on Wednesday, another sign that companies have to keep spending on security.

The stock now sits at Wall Street's average price target, but it still trades far below its own historical multiple. That makes it a long-term buy if late-November results hold up.

Zscaler (ZS:NASDAQ) lost its sales chief last month, and the stock fell 10% in a day. But it's already gained all that back and more – it's up 14% in the past month, while the Nasdaq 100 slipped 2%.

The "down" reaction made sense at the time. Rich built the account-focused sales overhaul that pushed net new ARR growth to 17% in the fiscal fourth quarter, up from 7% in fiscal 2025. And CFO Kevin Rubin had already blamed part of the cautious fiscal 2027 guide on sales leadership changes.

But then Investor Day won it all back

At its Oct. 6 Investor Day, Zscaler reaffirmed its guidance, including revenue growth of 16.6% to 17.5% for fiscal 2027. It also set a base case of more than $8 billion of ARR by fiscal 2031, more than double where it ended fiscal 2026.

"The agentic AI era is quickly becoming the most significant opportunity in our company's history," said CEO Jay Chaudhry.

Eleven firms raised their price targets the next morning, from Evercore ISI's $195 to Baird's $285. The stock rose 19% over the five sessions through Oct. 9. The run ended with a 7.8% jump that day, when CrowdStrike (CRWD:NASDAQ) and Palo Alto Networks (PANW:NASDAQ) gained about 4% each.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Zscaler, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Zscaler's Analyst Ratings

Hackers keep making the bull case

Zscaler fell 5.9% on Oct. 16 as software stocks sold off on worries about AI funding.

On Wednesday, it jumped 7.8% with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto and the rest of the group. The team behind the PHP programming language had just fixed two critical flaws that let attackers run their own code on web servers. Attacks started before the patch was out.

That's the gap Zscaler's new tool with IBM and Red Hat targets: the stretch between a flaw going public and the fix going in. As long as attackers keep getting better, "companies will keep having to pay for defensive cyber capabilities," Bloomberg's Joe Weisenthal wrote on X.

Investing.com -- SK Hynix's U.S.-listed ADRs could win a spot in the Nasdaq 100 if the chipmaker expands its ADR float, according to Goldman Sachs.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

The firm flagged the company's Oct. 28 earnings as a key catalyst.

The bank explained that the ADR initial listing represented only about 2.5% of SK Hynix's circulating equity.

At roughly $25.5 billion, the ADR currently sits between ranks 98 and 108 of eligible companies, leaving inclusion vulnerable to swings in peer mega-cap tech stocks. Goldman noted that an outside candidate typically needs an ADR valuation of $28 billion to $32 billion to safely make the cut.

"Expanding float to 5%–10% is necessary to unlock estimated long-term passive inflows of around $15 billion via the Nasdaq 100 (100) and Nasdaq Composite (3,000+)," Goldman wrote.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

The bank added that doubling the ADR pool to 5% would lift the U.S. listing's value to about $51 billion. That would place SK Hynix in the top 45 to 55 eligible issuers.

Under Nasdaq rules, any non-constituent ranked in the top 75 enters the index automatically. The annual reconstitution will be announced on Dec. 11 and take effect after Dec. 18.

Goldman noted that the ADR trades at a 47% premium to the Seoul shares. Its derivatives team suggests buying an ADR put funded by selling a Seoul put to capture any narrowing.

"With so much cash on the balance sheet and so much cashflow generation forecast, investors would likely not react well to a further ADR primary issuance," the firm said.

Goldman pointed instead to TSMC's expansion of its ADR float between 2003 and 2007 as a possible template.

Investing.com - U.S. stock index futures fell sharply on Thursday as investors assessed quarterly results from Meta Platforms and Tesla, while renewed concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending weighed on technology shares.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

The earnings reports put the focus on whether heavy investments in AI infrastructure, robotics and autonomous driving can deliver sufficient returns.

By 07:16 ET, S&P 500 futures had fallen 1.1%, Nasdaq 100 futures had dropped 1.7%, and Dow futures had retreated 0.7%.

Meta Platforms shares fell more than 1% in premarket trading despite the Facebook and Instagram parent beating third-quarter revenue and earnings estimates and forecasting stronger-than-expected revenue for the current quarter. Revenue rose 26% year over year to $64.60 billion, ahead of the $63.33 billion consensus, while earnings per share came in at $3.83, compared with estimates of $3.57. Advertising revenue also climbed 26% to $63.06 billion, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg saying engagement on Facebook and Instagram had reached record levels.

Meta forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion, above expectations at the midpoint, but raised its annual capital spending outlook to $135 billion-$145 billion from $130 billion-$145 billion as it continues investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Earnings also included a $9.89 billion legal charge related to a settlement with 52 state attorneys general over teen mental health litigation.

Tesla shares dropped 5.0% in premarket trading to $367.20 as investors reacted to the company's outlook for spending, vehicle sales and future growth. The electric-vehicle maker reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.48, beating estimates of around $0.43-$0.44, while free cash flow reached $1.53 billion, well above expectations.

However, net income attributable to common shareholders fell 29% year over year to $787 million, and automotive revenue declined 3% amid lower average selling prices and battery supply constraints.

Tesla also cut its full-year capital expenditure forecast to around $20 billion from more than $25 billion, raising questions about the pace of its AI and robotics investments. CEO Elon Musk said the company was targeting 5 million vehicle sales by the end of the decade, well below his earlier projection of 20 million. Tesla expects to begin shipping Optimus humanoid robots to corporate customers by the end of 2027, while meaningful robotaxi revenue is not expected until 2027-2028.

Investing.com - Futures linked to the main U.S. stock indices slip, as traders pore through earnings from Facebook-owner Meta Platforms and Elon Musk-led electric car giant Tesla. Meta shares advance in extended-hours trading after the tech behemoth unveils better-than-expected quarterly revenue and robust current-quarter guidance. Shares of Tesla fall on a lower annual sales target, while some insiders reportedly express concerns over regulatory scrutiny of a possible merger between Tesla and Musk's rocket firm SpaceX.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

1. Futures dip

U.S. stock futures pointed lower on Thursday. By 03:08 ET (07:08 GMT), the S&P 500 futures contract had fallen by 75 points, or 1.0%, Nasdaq 100 futures had dropped by 510 points, or 1.7%, and Dow futures had retreated by 283 points, or 0.5%.

The main averages on Wall Street advanced in the prior session, buoyed by strong results from Musk's rocket company SpaceX and server maker Super Micro Computer. The returns helped to assuage some recent concerns around the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade, although analysts at Deutsche Bank flagged that the decline in Nasdaq futures could be a sign that not all investors were reassured.

Jitters have surrounded the AI sector for several days, triggered by a combination of heavy debt-fueled spending on AI infrastructure and elevated borrowing costs. Roller-coaster movements in AI-exposed stocks have mirrored shifting sentiment around AI, especially after fresh corporate returns appear to indicate that demand for the nascent technology remains solid.

2. Meta rises after revenue beat

Shares of Meta crept higher in extended-hours trading after the Instagram-owner unveiled higher-than-anticipated third-quarter revenue and announced plans to create a new class of nonvoting stock to raise capital for its AI ambitions.

Along with resilience in its core advertising business, the well-received debut of Meta's Muse AI assistant in September has helped bolster returns during a time when the tech titan is investing hundreds of billions of dollars into the AI race. Hopes have been high that Muse will eventually add $28.5 billion of incremental revenue by 2030, according to Truist Securities projections cited by the Wall Street Journal.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in a post-earnings call that roughly a fourth of people who have set up Muse use it on "any given day," particularly for shopping. Zuckerberg added that Meta is aiming to create a "large-scale Muse network," even though the app has been blocked on some websites, such as Amazon.com.
